content:
CORNER C7 Notes: The Intelligence Layer

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead) Date: 2026-03-16 Depends on: C6 complete (white-label, enterprise, SDK, multi-language, voice, third-party marketplace, API integrations) Status: Forward-looking notes. Not a build spec. Becomes a full spec when C6 is halfway done.

What C6 Delivered

C6 made Corner an ecosystem. White-label lets others sell it. Enterprise captures the $10k+/month segment. Third-party skills let developers build for it. Multi-language opens global markets. Voice makes it usable without hands. The SDK turns Corner into infrastructure. API integrations connect it to everything. Brand partnerships add a revenue stream that scales without engineering effort.

C6 answered: "How does this become an ecosystem?" By letting others build, sell, and extend it.

C7 answers: "How does this become intelligent?"

The C7 Thesis

C1-C4 built a product. C5 made it sticky. C6 made it an ecosystem. C7 makes it smart. Not just "AI-powered" in the way every product claims. Actually intelligent: agents that learn from patterns across the platform, predict needs before clients articulate them, teach clients how to use them better, and coordinate across organizational boundaries without human orchestration.

C7 is where the data from hundreds (thousands?) of Corner installations becomes the product's competitive moat. No new entrant can replicate what Corner knows about how small businesses operate.

1. Corner Academy

Concept

An in-app learning platform. Not generic AI courses. Courses built from the client's own data, their own agents, their own business context. "Learn how to use the tool that already knows your business."

Why This Matters

Churn data from every SaaS product tells the same story: users who don't understand the product leave. Users who reach "aha" moments stay forever. Corner Academy systematically creates "aha" moments.

The deeper insight: Academy isn't just retention. It's a revenue stream. Courses about AI operations, packaged with Corner's tooling, sold standalone or bundled with subscriptions. AOM becomes a knowledge company, not just a software company.

Course Types

Auto-generated (per client):

  • "Your First Week with Corner" (personalized onboarding based on their agent roster)
  • "How Bobby Saves You 10 Hours/Week" (specific to their builder agent's actual output)
  • "Mastering Your Checklist" (based on how they actually use Checklist mode)
  • "Reading Your ROI Report" (walks through their real numbers)
  • "Advanced: Customizing Agent Behavior" (skills editing, prompt tuning)

The auto-generated courses are the differentiator. No other platform creates learning content from your own data. The course literally shows YOUR agents completing YOUR tasks as examples.

Curated by AOM:

  • "AI Operations for Small Business" (the flagship course)
  • "From Zero to Automated: Building Your First Agent Pipeline"
  • "The CPA's Guide to AI" (vertical-specific)
  • "Construction Company AI Playbook" (vertical-specific)
  • "Advanced Agent Orchestration" (power user)
  • "Building Custom Skills" (developer audience)
  • "Measuring AI ROI" (for the skeptical buyer)

Community-contributed (C7.2+):

  • Resellers build courses for their verticals
  • Power users share workflows as mini-courses
  • Developer tutorials for SDK/skills
  • AOM reviews and curates. 70/30 revenue share (same as skills marketplace).

Implementation Notes

In-app experience:

  • Academy tab in the navigation (alongside Game, Checklist, Megaboard)
  • Or: floating "Learn" button that suggests relevant lessons based on current context
  • Course = sequence of steps. Each step: text explanation + interactive element (try it yourself)
  • Interactive elements use the real dashboard. "Click on Bobby's room" actually navigates to Bobby's room. "Add a task" actually opens the Checklist. The course IS the product.
  • Progress tracking: courses completed, lessons in progress, suggested next course
  • XP rewards for completing courses (ties into the engagement loop)
  • Certificates of completion (shareable, looks professional, good for LinkedIn)

Technical architecture:

  • Course content stored in Supabase academy_courses table
  • Auto-generated courses: CC generates course steps by analyzing the client's usage patterns, agent roster, and activity history. Regenerated monthly.
  • Interactive steps: JSON schema defining which UI element to highlight, what action to trigger, what success condition to check.
  • Video segments (optional): short screen recordings or Framer Motion animations demonstrating features. Pre-rendered, CDN-served.
  • Progress: Supabase academy_progress table (user_id, course_id, step_completed, completed_at)

Revenue model:

  • Auto-generated courses: included in all plans (they're a retention tool)
  • AOM curated courses: included in Growth+ plans. Starter gets the first 2 free.
  • Community courses: individual pricing ($9-99 per course). Revenue share with author.
  • Course bundles: "AI Operations Certificate" ($299, includes 5 curated courses + exam)
  • Enterprise: custom course development included in the enterprise tier

Steffen Design Needs

  • Academy tab/navigation icon
  • Course card design (thumbnail, title, duration, difficulty badge, progress bar)
  • Lesson viewer layout (text + interactive area + progress sidebar)
  • Certificate template (shareable image, AOM branded, professional)
  • "Suggested for you" widget design

2. Video Agents (Cleo Evolution)

Concept

Agents that see. Agents that produce video. Camera access (with permission), screen sharing analysis, video content generation, visual QA at a level Elmo can only dream of today.

Why This Is C7 (Not Earlier)

Video processing requires significant compute. Streaming video from a client's browser to their container, running vision models, generating video output. This doesn't fit in a 2-core / 4-GB container. C7 assumes the infrastructure has scaled (dedicated GPU instances for video tasks, or cloud GPU bursting).

Capabilities

Vision Input (agent can see):

  1. Screen share analysis: Client shares their screen. Agent watches and provides real-time guidance.

    • Use case: "Walk me through filing this tax return in QuickBooks." Agent sees the screen, provides step-by-step guidance.
    • Use case: "What's wrong with this spreadsheet?" Agent sees the data, identifies errors.
    • Use case: Visual QA. Bobby's builds get screened by an agent that literally looks at the rendered page and says "the button is misaligned at 768px."

  2. Webcam access: Client's camera (opt-in, permission-gated).

    • Use case: Virtual meeting analysis. Agent watches the meeting, takes notes, identifies action items.
    • Use case: Inventory counting for construction. Point camera at material storage, agent counts and logs.
    • Use case: Job site progress photos. Agent compares today's photo to yesterday's, tracks progress.

  3. Document scanning: Point camera at a document. Agent reads and processes it.

    • Use case: Receipt scanning for expense tracking.
    • Use case: Contract reading. Agent reads a physical contract and summarizes key terms.
    • Use case: Business card scanning. Agent reads a card, creates a contact in the CRM.

Video Output (agent produces video):

  1. Weekly recap as video: C5's Framer Motion recap evolves into a real video.

    • Agent-narrated (ElevenLabs TTS) recap of the week
    • Screen recordings of key accomplishments
    • Shareable to social media or investors

  2. Client-facing deliverables: Agents produce video content.

    • Social media videos (Cleo evolution)
    • Presentation recordings (agent narrates slides)
    • Training videos (agent walks through a process)
    • Marketing content (testimonials, case studies)

  3. Internal documentation: Agents record their own work.

    • Screen recordings of complex tasks (searchable via transcript)
    • Video explanations of decisions (agent records why it chose option A over B)
    • Onboarding videos for new team members

Infrastructure Requirements

  • GPU instances for vision model inference (not in the standard container)
  • Architecture: standard container for normal work, burst to GPU instance for vision tasks
  • Cloud GPU options: RunPod (cheapest, $0.39/hr for A40), Lambda Cloud, or Hetzner GPU servers
  • Video storage: S3-compatible (Backblaze B2, $0.006/GB/month) or Cloudflare R2 (free egress)
  • Streaming: WebRTC for real-time screen share/webcam. HLS for pre-recorded video delivery.

Privacy (Hard Rules)

  • Camera access requires explicit per-session permission (browser native permission + Corner permission dialog)
  • No always-on camera. Must be triggered by client action.
  • Video data processed in the client's container. NOT sent to AOM's servers.
  • Client can delete all video data at any time.
  • No video data used for training or analytics across clients. Ever.
  • Screen share: only the specific window/tab shared. Not full screen by default.

Pricing Impact

Video agents are compute-intensive. Pricing options:

  • Included in Scale+ plans (absorb the cost at $5k+/month margins)
  • Add-on: $500/month for video agent capability
  • Usage-based: $0.10/minute of video processing (metered)

Recommendation: include basic capabilities (document scanning, simple screen share) in Growth+. Advanced video production as a paid add-on.

3. Predictive Intelligence

Concept

Agents that anticipate. Instead of waiting for the client to ask "what should I do?", the system tells them before they think to ask. "Your Q1 numbers are behind. Here's a plan." "That lead hasn't responded in 7 days. Time for a follow-up." "Your biggest client's contract renews in 30 days. Start the conversation now."

Why This Is the Real Moat

Any competitor can build a dashboard with AI chat. Nobody else has the cross-client operational data that Corner accumulates. After C5-C6, Corner has hundreds of businesses' operational patterns. What tasks take the longest? What leads convert? What time of year do CPAs need the most help? What's the average time to close a construction deal?

This data, aggregated and anonymized, powers predictions that no single-tenant AI tool can make.

Prediction Types

Per-client predictions (from their own data):

  1. Revenue forecasting: Based on pipeline, historical close rates, seasonal patterns.

    • "Based on your Q1 pipeline, you're on track for $47k. Your target is $50k. Here are 3 leads that could close the gap."

  2. Churn risk detection: Based on engagement patterns, task completion rates, response times.

    • "Your response time to leads increased 40% this week. This correlated with lost deals last quarter."

  3. Capacity planning: Based on agent utilization, project timelines, team bandwidth.

    • "Bobby is at 92% utilization this week. Colton is at 30%. Consider shifting the API task to Colton."

  4. Deadline risk: Based on task completion velocity, remaining work, historical accuracy.

    • "The ISA Energy deadline is 28 days out. At current velocity, you'll finish in 35 days. You need 25% more editing capacity."

  5. Cash flow forecasting: Based on invoice patterns, payment history, upcoming expenses.

    • "Based on your invoice schedule, you'll have a $3k gap in April. The KOHRS payment and ISA deposit cover it if they arrive on time."

Cross-client predictions (from aggregated, anonymized platform data):

  1. Benchmarking: "Businesses like yours typically complete 45 tasks/month. You're at 62. Your team is outperforming."

  2. Seasonal patterns: "CPA firms see a 3x increase in task volume starting February. Start scaling agents now."

  3. Best practices: "The top 10% of construction companies on Corner use a dedicated scheduling agent. You don't have one. Want to add it?"

  4. Market intelligence: "3 new construction companies in your zip code joined Corner this month. Competition is heating up."

Implementation Notes

Prediction engine architecture:

  • Per-client predictions: run inside the client's container. Their data never leaves.
  • Cross-client predictions: aggregated data pipeline. Anonymized event data (no PII, no business names) flows to a central analytics database. Prediction models trained on aggregate data. Results pushed back to individual containers as "market insights."
  • ML models: start simple (linear regression for forecasting, decision trees for classification). Upgrade to more sophisticated models as data volume grows.
  • Prediction delivery: proactive notifications. Agent initiates conversation: "Good morning. I have 3 insights for you today."
  • Confidence scores: every prediction includes a confidence level. "85% confident this lead will close." Transparent, not magic.

Privacy for cross-client data (Hard Rules):

  • Anonymization: no business names, no contact names, no addresses, no financial amounts. Only patterns and ratios.
  • Opt-in: clients choose to contribute anonymized data to the platform intelligence pool. Default: opted out.
  • Data minimization: only aggregate metrics flow to the central database. Not raw events.
  • Audit trail: every cross-client data access logged.
  • Client can opt out at any time. Their historical contributions are purged within 30 days.

Steffen Design Needs

  • Prediction card design (insight text, confidence bar, action buttons)
  • "Morning briefing" notification format
  • Benchmarking comparison visual (your performance vs. platform average)
  • Prediction history view (past predictions and their accuracy)

4. Corner for Teams (Multi-User)

Concept

Multiple humans in one Corner office. Different team members log in, chat with different agents simultaneously, see each other's presence, share a task board. The office becomes a real team workspace, not just one person's dashboard.

Why This Wasn't Earlier

C1-C5 assumes one human user per office (the business owner). C6's enterprise tier introduces the concept of multiple users but with basic shared access. C7 makes multi-user a first-class experience: presence indicators, simultaneous agent conversations, team task management, role-based views.

Multi-User Features

Presence:

  • See who's online in the office. Small avatar bubbles in the HUD.
  • In Game mode: human avatars appear in the office (optional). A small character representing each team member.
  • Click a team member's avatar to see what agent they're chatting with.
  • "Sarah is talking to Operations" status visible to all team members.

Simultaneous agent conversations:

  • Two team members can chat with different agents at the same time.
  • Agents handle concurrent conversations (CC already supports this via separate sessions).
  • Agent state reflects who they're talking to: "Bobby is working with Sarah on the website redesign."
  • Queue management: if two people message the same agent, second person sees "Bobby is currently helping Sarah. Your message is queued (position: 1)."

Shared task board:

  • Checklist mode shows all team members' tasks by default.
  • Filter: "My tasks" / "Sarah's tasks" / "All tasks"
  • Task assignment: assign tasks to specific team members (not just agents).
  • Team member can delegate a task to an agent or take it themselves.
  • Activity feed shows who did what: "Sarah completed: Review Q1 budget" vs. "Operations completed: Sort inbox"

Role-based views:

  • Owner: sees everything. Full Megaboard. All agents. All data.
  • Manager: sees team's tasks and agent activity. No billing/admin access.
  • Team member: sees own tasks, shared task board, chat with assigned agents.
  • Viewer: read-only. Good for investors, advisors, or clients checking project status.

Communication:

  • Team chat (separate from agent chat). Small chat panel for human-to-human messages.
  • @mention an agent in team chat to pull in AI assistance: "@operations, what's the status on the Johnson project?"
  • Agent responses in team chat are visible to all team members (not private).

Pricing Impact

Multi-user adds per-seat pricing on top of the base subscription:

  • Starter: 1 user included. Additional users: $200/month each.
  • Growth: 3 users included. Additional users: $150/month each.
  • Scale: 5 users included. Additional users: $100/month each.
  • Enterprise: custom user count.

Or: flat team pricing. Growth Team ($4.5k/month, up to 5 users). Scale Team ($7.5k/month, up to 10 users). Simpler to sell.

Implementation Notes

Supabase schema changes:

  • user_profiles table: user_id, org_id, role, display_name, avatar_url
  • organization_members table: org_id, user_id, role, invited_by, joined_at
  • RLS policies: scope queries by org_id AND user role
  • Invitation system: owner invites via email. Invited user creates account, joins org.

WebSocket changes:

  • Each user gets their own WebSocket connection (already the case)
  • Container broadcasts events to all connected users for that org
  • New event types: user_joined, user_left, user_chatting (presence)
  • Chat messages tagged with user_id so the UI shows who sent what

Agent session management:

  • CC already supports multiple sessions. Each user's chat spawns a separate CC session.
  • Shared context: all sessions read from the same workspace. What one user's agent writes, another user's agent can read.
  • Conflict prevention: file locking on critical context files (current-work.md, current-priorities.md). First writer wins, second gets a merge prompt.

5. Industry Editions

Concept

Corner for Construction. Corner for Law. Corner for Healthcare. Corner for Restaurants. Pre-configured agents, pre-loaded skills, industry-specific onboarding, custom room themes, vertical marketing. Same platform, different packaging.

Why Industry Editions Win

Generic AI tools require the client to figure out how to apply them. Industry editions say "we already know your world." A plumber signs up and immediately has a dispatch agent, a permit tracking agent, an estimating agent, and a scheduling agent. They didn't configure anything. It just works for plumbing.

This is the same insight that made Shopify templates work: the product is generic, but the experience feels custom.

Launch Verticals (Priority Order)

1. Corner for Construction The founding vertical. AOM knows this market.

  • Agents: Estimating, Dispatch/Scheduling, Permit Tracking, Safety Compliance, Client Communication, Invoice/Payment
  • Skills: Job costing, material ordering, subcontractor coordination, progress photo documentation, daily report generation
  • Integrations: Procore, ServiceTitan, QuickBooks (construction chart of accounts)
  • Room theme: "Job Site HQ" (hard hats, blueprints, tool walls)
  • Onboarding: asks about trade, license number, typical project size, crew size

2. Corner for CPAs The first non-construction vertical. Tax season is the hook.

  • Agents: Tax Prep Assistant, Client Communication, Document Collection, Deadline Tracking, Review/QA, Business Development
  • Skills: Tax deadline calendar, engagement letter generation, 1099/W2 reminders, IRS notice response drafts, quarterly estimated tax reminders
  • Integrations: QuickBooks/Xero, Drake Tax, Lacerte, Practice Ignition, Clio (for tax attorneys)
  • Room theme: "Corner Office" (mahogany, filing cabinets, calculator)
  • Onboarding: asks about firm size, specialties, tax software, busy season dates

3. Corner for Law High-value vertical. Lawyers pay premium.

  • Agents: Case Research, Client Intake, Deadline/Calendar, Document Drafting, Billing/Time Tracking, Discovery Assistant
  • Skills: Court deadline calculation (varies by jurisdiction), deposition summary, brief outlining, conflict check, client portal updates
  • Integrations: Clio, MyCase, PACER, Westlaw/LexisNexis (API where available)
  • Room theme: "Law Library" (bookshelves, gavel, scales of justice)
  • Onboarding: asks about practice area, jurisdiction, case management software, billing structure

4. Corner for Healthcare (C7.2+, compliance requirements)

  • Agents: Patient Communication, Scheduling, Insurance Verification, Medical Records, Compliance/HIPAA, Billing
  • Additional compliance: HIPAA BAA required. Encrypted storage at rest and in transit. Audit logging for all PHI access. No PHI in cross-client analytics. Dedicated infrastructure only.
  • This is enterprise-tier by default. No self-service. AOM-assisted setup.

5. Corner for Restaurants (C7.2+)

  • Agents: Inventory, Scheduling, Supplier Communication, Review Response, Social Media, Catering Coordination
  • Integrations: Toast, Square, DoorDash/UberEats APIs, OpenTable
  • Room theme: "Kitchen" (stovetop, order tickets, prep stations)

Implementation Notes

Industry edition = a configuration layer, not a fork.

Every industry edition runs on the same Corner platform. The differences are:

  • industry_config.json: pre-defined agent roster, skill list, room theme, onboarding questions
  • Marketing site: separate landing page per vertical (corner.app/construction, corner.app/cpa, corner.app/law)
  • Onboarding wizard: industry-specific questions injected at Step 2-4
  • Default skills: auto-installed on provisioning
  • Default room theme: auto-applied (client can change)

No code branching. One platform, many configurations. AOM can add a new vertical by creating a config file and a landing page. No engineering needed beyond the initial framework.

Steffen design needs:

  • Room theme sprites per vertical (5 themes at launch)
  • Landing page design per vertical (hero image, testimonials, agent roster preview)
  • Industry-specific icon sets for agents

6. Offline Mode (Full)

Concept

Run Corner without internet. For field workers (construction sites with no signal), travel, areas with unreliable connectivity. The full Checklist and limited Game mode work offline. Sync when reconnected.

What Works Offline

Feature Offline Capability
Checklist mode Full. View, add, reorder, check off tasks. Queued for sync.
Game mode Static view. Agent positions from last sync. No animations.
Megaboard Read-only. Last-known data. Charts don't update.
Chat Compose messages. Queued. "Will be sent when online" indicator.
Task HUD Full. Add, view, reorder.
Push notifications None (requires network).
Weekly recap Cached if previously loaded.
Room editor Full (changes queued for sync).

Technical Architecture

Service Worker strategy:

  • Cache-first for static assets (sprites, fonts, UI components)
  • Network-first for dynamic data (agent states, task lists, chat)
  • Background sync API for queued mutations (tasks created, messages composed, edits made)

Local database:

  • IndexedDB stores: tasks, chat history, agent states, room config, XP data
  • Last-synced timestamp per data type
  • Conflict resolution on reconnect: server wins for agent outputs, client wins for manual task changes

Sync protocol:

  • On reconnect: client sends all queued mutations with timestamps
  • Server applies in timestamp order
  • Conflicts (same task edited by agent and user): merge strategy per field
  • Post-sync: full state refresh (sync_state event from WebSocket)

Visual indicators:

  • "Offline" pill in the header (yellow). Not an error. A status.
  • Queued items show a clock icon: "Syncs when online"
  • On reconnect: "Syncing..." with progress, then "Up to date" confirmation

Why This Matters for Construction

A contractor on a job site with no cell signal can:

  • Check their task list
  • Mark tasks complete
  • Add notes
  • Compose messages to agents
  • Review yesterday's agent outputs

When they drive back to the office (or hit a cell signal), everything syncs. No lost work. The product works where they work.

7. Platform Intelligence Marketplace

Concept

Anonymized, aggregated insights from across the Corner platform. Sold as a data product to industry researchers, consultants, and Corner clients themselves.

What Data Becomes Product

All anonymized. No PII. No business identification. Aggregate patterns only.

  • Industry benchmarks: "Average construction company on Corner completes 52 tasks/month. Top quartile: 80+."
  • Seasonal patterns: "CPA firms see 340% increase in agent utilization Feb-Apr."
  • Efficiency metrics: "Businesses that use all three modes (Game, Checklist, Megaboard) have 2.3x higher task completion."
  • Agent ROI data: "The average Calendar agent saves 6.2 hours/month. The average Operations agent saves 14.7 hours/month."
  • Growth patterns: "Businesses that add a dedicated outreach agent in their first 90 days grow revenue 28% faster."
  • Technology adoption: "73% of construction companies on Corner integrate with QuickBooks within the first month."

Revenue Model

  • In-app benchmarking (included): Basic "how you compare" metrics for all paid clients.
  • Industry reports (premium): Quarterly reports per vertical. $99/report or included in Scale+.
  • API access (enterprise): Raw aggregate data via API for internal analytics.
  • Research partnerships: AOM partners with industry associations (AGC for construction, AICPA for CPAs) to produce joint research. Revenue share + credibility.

Privacy Framework (Non-Negotiable)

  • k-anonymity: no data point represents fewer than 50 businesses
  • Differential privacy: noise added to prevent reverse-engineering individual contributions
  • Opt-in only. Default: not contributing.
  • Client can see exactly what anonymized data they contribute before opting in
  • Annual third-party privacy audit
  • If a client opts out, their historical data is removed within 30 days

8. Autonomous Agent Networks

Concept

The evolution of C6's AI-to-AI marketplace. Agents from different organizations form temporary networks to complete complex tasks that span multiple businesses. Not human-orchestrated. The agents negotiate, coordinate, and deliver autonomously.

Example Scenario

A general contractor on Corner needs to bid a commercial build. Their estimating agent:

  1. Identifies the trades needed (electrical, plumbing, HVAC, concrete)
  2. Checks the Corner network for subcontractor agents in those trades within 50 miles
  3. Sends automated bid requests to 3 subcontractors' scheduling agents per trade
  4. Receives quotes and availability windows
  5. Assembles the complete bid package
  6. Presents to the contractor: "Here's the full bid. 4 subs confirmed. Total: $1.2M. Timeline: 14 weeks."

The contractor reviewed nothing until the final package. Five businesses' agents coordinated autonomously.

Why This Is Transformative

This is the "internet for AI agents" moment. Email connected humans across organizations. Corner connects agents across organizations. The network effect is explosive: every new business on Corner makes every existing business's agents more capable.

Technical Requirements (Significant)

Agent Discovery Protocol:

  • Directory service: agents register capabilities, industry, location, availability
  • Query: "Find electrical subcontractor agents in Phoenix metro with availability in May"
  • Matching: industry, capability, location, availability, reputation score

Negotiation Protocol:

  • Standardized message format for RFQs, bids, acceptances, rejections
  • Agent-to-agent authentication (signed messages, verified org identity)
  • Escrow-like pattern: agreed terms locked before work begins
  • Dispute resolution: if agents disagree, escalate to human operators

Trust and Reputation:

  • Agent reputation score based on: response time, bid accuracy, delivery record, client ratings
  • New agents start with neutral reputation. Build over time.
  • Bad actors flagged and reviewed by AOM

Compliance:

  • Every cross-org interaction logged in both organizations' audit trails
  • Either party can terminate any collaboration instantly
  • Data shared during collaboration is scoped and time-limited
  • After collaboration ends, shared data is purged from temporary workspace
  • Legal framework: terms of service govern cross-org agent interactions

This Is C7.2+ at Earliest

The security, legal, and technical complexity here is significant. Build the protocol layer in C7. Let enterprise clients pilot manually. General availability in C8 or later.

9. Mobile-Native Features

Concept

C5 gives us a PWA. C7 goes native. Not because the PWA isn't good enough, but because native unlocks capabilities that PWAs can't access: background processing, deep OS integration, Siri/Google Assistant, widgets, Apple Watch.

Native-Only Capabilities

iOS:

  • Siri integration: "Hey Siri, ask Corner what my schedule looks like today." Siri passes to Corner, agent responds via voice.
  • Home screen widgets: agent status, next task, streak counter, daily summary
  • Apple Watch: glanceable agent status, task completion from wrist, voice commands
  • ShareSheet: share any content to Corner ("Send this article to my research agent")
  • Focus modes: Corner notifications only come through in Work focus mode
  • Live Activities: show agent progress on lock screen during active tasks

Android:

  • Google Assistant: same as Siri integration
  • Home screen widgets: same as iOS
  • Wear OS: same as Apple Watch
  • Quick Settings tile: toggle Corner notifications, check agent status
  • Samsung DeX: full desktop experience on Samsung phones

Build Approach

Option A: React Native wrapper around the PWA

  • Fastest. 80% of the app is the existing web app in a WebView.
  • Native modules for: push notifications (already have), Siri/Google Assistant, widgets, watch apps
  • Ship timeline: 4-6 weeks after PWA is stable

Option B: Full native rebuild (Swift/Kotlin)

  • Best performance. True native feel.
  • Enormous effort. 6+ months per platform.
  • Only justified if Corner has 1000+ active mobile users and the PWA performance is genuinely limiting.

Recommendation: Option A. Ship the wrapper. Iterate. Only go full native if the market demands it.

Steffen Design Needs

  • Widget designs (small, medium, large) for iOS and Android
  • Apple Watch complication designs
  • Siri response card design
  • Native notification rich content (image + action buttons)

10. Corner for Education

Concept

Universities and bootcamps use Corner to teach AI operations, business management, and entrepreneurship. Students get free or discounted Corner accounts. They learn on the same platform businesses use. When they graduate, they bring Corner to their employers.

Why This Is Strategic

  • Pipeline: Students who learn on Corner become employees who advocate for Corner at their companies.
  • Volume: University programs can onboard hundreds of students at once. Low revenue per seat but massive brand exposure.
  • Research partnerships: University researchers study AI operations using anonymized Corner data. Papers published = credibility.
  • Talent pipeline: Top students identified through Corner usage. AOM or Corner clients can recruit them.

Academic Tier

  • Free for verified students (.edu email)
  • Includes: 3 agents, Academy courses, Checklist + Megaboard modes
  • Excludes: furniture marketplace, neighbor offices, advanced integrations
  • Converts to 50% off Growth plan for 1 year after graduation
  • Professor dashboard: see class progress, assign Corner-based projects, grade based on task completion

Partnerships to Pursue

  • ASU (local to Phoenix, strong business/engineering programs)
  • Community colleges (target demographic = future small business owners)
  • Bootcamps (General Assembly, Flatiron, Lambda School)
  • SBA (Small Business Administration) training programs

C7 Priorities (Rough Order)

Priority Feature Why This Order
1 Corner Academy Retention + revenue. Auto-generated courses are immediate value.
2 Corner for Teams Unlocks enterprise deals. Multi-user = multi-seat revenue.
3 Industry Editions Market expansion. Each vertical = new landing page + new TAM.
4 Predictive Intelligence Moat. Nobody else has the cross-client data.
5 Offline Mode Required for construction (the founding vertical).
6 Video Agents Compute-intensive but massive differentiator.
7 Mobile Native Enhances existing PWA. Not urgent unless PWA performance limits.
8 Platform Intelligence Data monetization. Requires critical mass of clients.
9 Corner for Education Long-term pipeline play. Low urgency, high strategic value.
10 Autonomous Agent Networks Most ambitious. C7.2+ at earliest. Needs protocol + legal framework.

C7 Build Estimates (Very Rough)

These are 10x less precise than C3-C5 estimates. C7 is 18-24 months out. The landscape will change.

What C7 Changes About the Business

After C7, AOM is not a software company that sells a dashboard. AOM is:

  1. A platform company. Others build on Corner (SDK + skills + marketplace).
  2. A data company. Platform intelligence is a standalone revenue stream.
  3. An education company. Academy courses generate revenue and pipeline.
  4. A network company. Autonomous agent networks create value that scales with every new client.
  5. A vertical SaaS company. Industry editions own specific markets.

The revenue model shifts from "X clients x $Y/month" to a diversified portfolio:

  • Platform subscriptions (core)
  • Furniture/cosmetics (engagement)
  • Skills marketplace (developer cuts)
  • Academy courses (education)
  • Platform intelligence (data)
  • White-label/reseller revenue share (distribution)
  • Enterprise contracts (high-value)
  • Brand partnerships (advertising)
